slides.title: Debugging
slides.say: Welcome. This chapter teaches four instruments for finding bugs: raise, assert, logging and the debugger. The same examples run on the chapter page.

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: Five parts: exceptions and tracebacks, assertions, logging, hunting bugs with the log, and the debugger.

slides.title: Two questions this chapter answers
slides.say: Two questions to carry through the chapter. Which instrument fits which problem? And which printed outputs of the book differ in current Python? The answers come back near the end.

slides.title: Part 1: Exceptions and tracebacks
slides.say: Part one. A function refuses a bad call with raise. The exception climbs the call stack, and the traceback is the report of that climb.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: errors and exceptions
slides.say: An exception is a fire alarm. Raise pulls the lever, the traceback shows the path the alarm took.

slides.title: Story: the bug you can visit in a museum
slides.say: The logbook page is dated 9 September 1947. The moth was taped in beside the joke about the first actual case of a bug.

slides.title: raise: a function refuses a bad call
slides.say: Box print refuses a call it cannot serve. Each raise stops the function and hands an Exception with a message to the caller.

slides.title: except ... as err: the exception object
slides.say: The message is kept in args. The except clause catches by class, and a more specific class is still an Exception. The diagram shows the family tree.

slides.title: The traceback: where an exception passed
slides.say: Nobody in read age, load or process claims the error, so it climbs to the try. The traceback lists the calls it passed, outermost first.

slides.title: add_note: context travels with the error
slides.say: Since Python 3.11 an exception can carry notes. The note is added where the context is known and printed after the message.

slides.title: Part 2: Assertions
slides.say: Part two. An assert is a tripwire for the programmer. It checks beliefs, not user input, and it disappears under python dash capital O.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: assertions
slides.say: An assertion is a tripwire set by the builder. It checks what must be true if the program is correct. It guards the programmer, never the user.

slides.title: assert: a check the programmer believes
slides.say: The assert states a belief and is silent when it holds. When it fails it raises AssertionError.

slides.title: assert for the programmer, raise for the user
slides.say: The user can pass an empty list, so we raise. Only our own bug can make a negative total, so we assert. The message is built only when the check fails.

slides.title: python -O removes every assert
slides.say: Under python dash O, assert statements are removed. That is why asserts guard the programmer and never the user. Compile with optimize equals one shows it.

slides.title: Part 3: Logging
slides.say: Part three. Logging leaves a record without stopping the program. Choose a level, a format and a destination, and switch it off without deleting a line.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: logging
slides.say: A log is a logbook. Each entry has a level, the format is the form, and the file is the notebook. Disable is the mute button.

slides.title: Story: the most effective debugging tool
slides.say: Kernighan wrote this in 1979. Thinking comes first, print statements second. Logging is the same idea with levels and an off switch.

slides.title: Story: a logging system with a birth certificate
slides.say: PEP 282 was created in February 2002 and landed in Python 2.3. The five levels are its design.

slides.title: Logging levels: five names, five numbers
slides.say: Five names, five numbers, from ten to fifty. A message is shown when its number reaches the threshold. Warning is the default threshold.

slides.title: basicConfig: choose what you hear
slides.say: One call to basicConfig sets the threshold, the format and the destination. With INFO the debug line stays silent. Force equals true replaces an earlier setup.

slides.title: The format string: what each line shows
slides.say: The format string names the fields of a line. To keep the result fixed, the record is built by hand. In a real program logging does that for you.

slides.title: filename=: evidence on disk
slides.say: The named parameter filename sends the log to a file. The screen stays quiet; the evidence stays on disk. A critical message still lands in the file.

slides.title: logging.disable: silence without deleting
slides.say: Disable silences a level and everything below it. Notset switches everything back on. No logging call has to be deleted.

slides.title: Arguments are formatted only when needed
slides.say: A message with arguments is formatted only if it is emitted. The f-string builds the text first, even when nobody reads it. Count the calls.

slides.title: Part 4: Hunting bugs with the log
slides.say: Part four. Three bugs from the chapter: a loop that starts too early, strings that were meant to be numbers, and a comparison that can never be true.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: hunting a bug
slides.say: Each of the three buggy programs hides one small mistake: a zero at the start, a string where a number belongs, a comparison across types.

slides.title: Hunt one bug with the log as witness
slides.say: Read the DEBUG lines: i starts at zero and total dies with it. The log is the witness that shows the loop starts one step too early.

slides.title: The one-character fix, witnessed
slides.say: Range from one to n plus one. The product grows one, two, six. The same log that found the bug now proves the fix.

slides.title: The string that beat the number
slides.say: Input gives text. Plus joins text. Five, three and forty-two become 5342. Convert each answer with int before adding.

slides.title: The coin toss that can never win
slides.say: The toss is a number and the guess is a text. They are never equal, so the game never lets you win. The tuple test only checks the spelling.

slides.title: Compare like with like
slides.say: Turn the number into its word before the comparison. Out of a thousand tosses the fixed game agrees about half the time; the buggy one never.

slides.title: Part 5: The debugger
slides.say: Part five. A debugger pauses the program and shows its variables. First see how it works inside, then the controls and the breakpoint call.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: the debugger
slides.say: A debugger pauses the film of the program. A breakpoint says where, the inspector shows the variables. The Mu editor is where the book shows it.

slides.title: Everyday pictures: the debugger controls
slides.say: Five controls: continue, step in, step over, step out and stop.

slides.title: The controls of the debugger
slides.say: Step in enters, step over skips, step out leaves.

slides.title: Inside a debugger: pause at every line
slides.say: A debugger is a program that watches another program line by line. Settrace gives us the same hook. The list is what an inspector pane would show at each pause.

slides.title: breakpoint() and the commands of pdb
slides.say: Breakpoint calls sys dot breakpointhook. Swap the hook and the call does something else. Pdb offers the editor's controls as commands.

slides.title: Choose the instrument by the question
slides.say: Choose by the question. Can the caller fix it? Raise. Must it always be true? Assert. What happened during the run? Log. What is the state at this line? Debugger.

slides.title: Current Python adds more
slides.say: Python moves on. Notes arrived in 3.11, better error locations in 3.11, and the safe attach to a running process in 3.14. The book does not cover these.

slides.title: Summary
slides.say: Five sentences to keep. The chart shows how many examples each part ran.

slides.title: Practice Questions
slides.say: Four drills. Predict first, then run on the page.

slides.title: Resources: where to go next
slides.say: Start with the book chapter, then the Python documentation. The stories link to first-hand sources. Choose one link and read it before the next class.
